lessons.title: Site Selection and Orientation
lessons.body:
Choosing the right site for your cold room is the first step to saving money on electricity and repairs. In Africa, the biggest enemy is the sun. A cold room that sits in full sun all day can use 30% more power than one in shade. So, look for a spot with natural shade from trees or buildings, or plan to build a shade roof. Also, avoid low-lying areas that flood during rainsâwater around the foundation causes rust and insulation damage. The ground should be level and well-drained. If you are in a city like Nairobi or Lagos, check for reliable electricity and water access. A backup generator or solar panels are smart if power cuts are common.

Orientation matters. In the northern hemisphere, the sun is in the south; in the southern hemisphere, it's in the north. But in Africa, the sun is mostly overhead. Still, morning and afternoon sun can hit east and west walls. Try to place the cold room so its longest walls face north and south, reducing direct sun on the walls. If that's not possible, use light-colored paint or reflective foil on the outside to bounce heat away. Also, keep the door away from direct sunlightâa door in the shade stays cooler and opens less often.

Think about access. You need a hard road for trucks to deliver goods. If the site is muddy, you'll struggle during rainy season. Also, consider future expansionâleave space to add another room or a loading dock. And don't forget security: a fence and good lighting deter thieves. Finally, check local regulations. In some areas, you need permits for commercial refrigeration. Talk to the local council early to avoid fines.

A good site saves you money every day. Spend time scouting. Visit the site at different times of day to see sun and water patterns. Talk to neighbors about flooding and power. A little planning now prevents big headaches later.

lessons.title: Insulation Materials and Thickness
lessons.body:
Insulation is the blanket that keeps cold air in and hot air out. Without it, your compressor runs non-stop and your electricity bill skyrockets. The most common insulation for cold rooms in Africa is polyurethane (PU) foam, either as rigid boards or sprayed-in-place. PU has high R-value (around 6 per inch), meaning it resists heat flow well. Other options include polystyrene (cheaper but lower R-value) and mineral wool (fire-resistant but absorbs moisture). For most small to medium cold rooms, PU panels are best.

Thickness depends on the temperature difference and your budget. For a chiller (0Â°C to 10Â°C), use 75â100 mm of PU. For a freezer (-18Â°C to -25Â°C), use 100â150 mm. In very hot climates like the Sahel, add 25 mm more. The math: heat gain = area Ã temperature difference Ã· R-value. So, a 10 mÂ² wall with 100 mm PU (Râ24) and 30Â°C outside vs 0Â°C inside gains about 12.5 watts per square meter. That adds up. Thicker insulation costs more upfront but pays back in lower power bills within 2â3 years.

Installation matters as much as material. Panels must fit tightly with no gaps. Use tongue-and-groove edges and seal joints with expanding foam or silicone. For sprayed foam, apply in layers to avoid voids. Never compress insulationâit loses R-value. Also, protect insulation from moisture: if it gets wet, it conducts heat and can grow mold. So, always install a vapor barrier on the warm side (more on that in Lesson 3).

In Africa, watch out for termites and rodents. They love to nest in polystyrene and sometimes PU. Use treated timber or metal framing, and keep insulation sealed. If you're on a tight budget, you can use locally made panels from a workshop, but check qualityâpoorly made panels leak cold. Ask for samples and test them. A simple test: put a piece in the sun; if it warps or smells, reject it. Good insulation is the heart of an efficient cold room.

lessons.title: Vapor Barriers and Air Tightness
lessons.body:
In cold storage, moisture is your enemy. Warm air holds water vapor. When that air hits a cold surface, it condenses into water, then ice. This ice blocks airflow, rusts metal, and ruins insulation. A vapor barrier stops moisture from entering the insulation. It's a thin sheetâusually polyethylene plastic (0.15â0.25 mm thick) or aluminum foilâplaced on the warm side of the insulation. In Africa, where humidity can be high, especially near coasts, a good vapor barrier is critical.

Install the vapor barrier on the outside of the insulation (the warm side). For a typical cold room, that means: outside wall, then vapor barrier, then insulation, then cold room interior. Seal all joints with special tape or adhesive. Overlap sheets by at least 150 mm. Use mastic around pipes, wires, and door frames. Any gap lets moist air in. A common mistake is to put the barrier on the cold sideâthat traps moisture inside and causes rot. Don't do it.

Air tightness goes hand in hand. Even tiny cracks let in warm, moist air. Use expanding foam to fill gaps around pipes. Install door seals (gaskets) that compress tightly. Check doors regularlyâif you can see light or feel a draft, replace the gasket. For walk-in doors, add a strip curtain or air curtain to reduce air exchange when the door opens. In dusty areas, keep the condenser coils clean; dust reduces airflow and efficiency.

To test for leaks, do a smoke test: light a incense stick and move it around joints and doors. If smoke blows away, there's a leak. Fix it immediately. Another test: on a hot day, feel for cold spots on the outside of the roomâthat's escaping cold. A well-sealed room should have no condensation on the outside. Remember, every leak costs you money. A 1 mm gap around a door can add 10% to your energy bill. So, take your time sealing. It's worth it.

lessons.title: Flooring and Drainage Systems
lessons.body:
The floor of your cold room must handle heavy loads, resist water, and be easy to clean. Concrete is the standard. Use a mix of 1:2:4 (cement:sand:aggregate) and reinforce with steel mesh if you'll store heavy pallets. The floor should slope slightly toward a drainâabout 1% slope (1 cm per meter). This lets wash water and defrost water flow away. Without a drain, water pools, causing ice and slips. In Africa, where floors may be uneven, take extra care to level.

Insulation under the floor is often overlooked. If you're building a freezer, you need insulation under the concrete to prevent frost heave and heat gain from the ground. Use 50â100 mm of PU or extruded polystyrene (XPS) under the slab. For chillers, you can skip under-floor insulation if the ground stays cool, but in hot climates, it's still a good idea. Also, add a vapor barrier under the slab to stop ground moisture. The floor finish should be smooth but not slippery. Epoxy or sealed concrete works well. Avoid tilesâthey crack and lift.

Drainage: install a floor drain at the lowest point. Use a trap to prevent sewer gases from entering. The drain pipe should be at least 50 mm diameter and slope to a gully outside. In areas with heavy rain, ensure the outside drainage carries water away from the building. If you can't install a floor drain, use a removable grate and a bucket, but that's less hygienic. For small rooms, a simple hole with a screen and a hose to outside can work.

Clean floors daily. Use a squeegee to push water to the drain. Don't let water sit. In fish and meat storage, blood and juices can clog drainsâuse a strainer. Also, keep the floor dry near doors to prevent ice. If you have a freezer, install a heater wire in the floor near the door to prevent frost. A well-designed floor and drainage system keeps your cold room safe and efficient.

lessons.title: Racking and Storage Configurations
lessons.body:
How you arrange goods inside a cold room affects airflow, safety, and how much you can store. The goal is to maximize space while allowing cold air to circulate around every product. Cold air is heavy and sinks, so you need space for it to flow. Don't stack boxes directly on the floorâuse pallets or shelves at least 100 mm off the floor. Also, leave 50â100 mm between rows and 150 mm from walls. This prevents warm spots and lets you check for pests.

Racking options: For small rooms, use plastic or metal shelving. For larger operations, use pallet racks. In Africa, where humidity can be high, choose galvanized steel or plastic to avoid rust. Wood can harbor mold. If you use wood, seal it with paint. Racks should be stableâanchor them to the floor or wall. Don't overload. Each shelf should have a load limit; check the manufacturer's specs. For heavy items like frozen meat, use heavy-duty racks.

Configuration: The layout should match your workflow. If you receive and dispatch often, place fast-moving items near the door. Use a U-shape or L-shape aisle to reduce travel. For freezers, keep doors closedâso organize so you can grab what you need quickly. Consider using bins or baskets for small items. Label everything. A common mistake is to fill the room so full that air can't circulate. That causes warm spots and spoilage. Leave at least 30% of the volume empty for air movement.

Also, think about safety. Heavy items on top shelves are dangerous. Put heavy items low. Keep aisles at least 1 meter wide for trolleys. If you have a walk-in, make sure the door can open fully. In small shops, you might use a chest freezer with basketsâsame rules apply: don't block vents. Regularly check that products are not blocking the evaporator fans. Good racking and layout reduce energy use and increase storage capacity. It's like a puzzleâplan it before you load.

lessons.title: Designing for Efficient Airflow
lessons.body:
Airflow is the bloodstream of your cold room. Without it, cold spots and warm spots form, and food spoils. The evaporator fan blows cold air, which must circulate around all products. Blocked airflow is the number one cause of uneven temperatures. So, design your room to let air move freely. First, position the evaporator unit correctly. It should be at one end, blowing air along the ceiling or down an aisle. Don't put it in a corner where air short-circuits back to the return. For small rooms, a ceiling-mounted unit works. For larger, use multiple units or a ducted system.

Aisle layout matters. Use a central aisle with racks on both sides. This lets air flow down the aisle and return along the walls. Leave a gap between the top of the racks and the ceilingâat least 300 mmâso air can flow over. Also, don't stack products higher than the evaporator fan level. If you have a freezer, use a fan to circulate air; natural convection is not enough. In Africa, where ambient temperatures are high, you need strong airflow. Aim for 10â20 air changes per hour for chillers, 20â30 for freezers.

Use air curtains or strip curtains on doors. Every time the door opens, warm air rushes in. A strip curtain reduces that by up to 70%. Also, consider a false ceiling or baffle to direct air. For rooms with high ceilings, install a false ceiling at 2.5â3 meters to keep cold air down where it's needed. Don't block the return air grilleâkeep it clear of boxes. If you notice some areas are warmer, add small fans to boost circulation. But don't overdo itâfans add heat. Use energy-efficient EC fans.

Test your airflow. Use a smoke pencil or a small tissue on a stick to see air movement. Or install a few thermometers at different heights and locations. If you see a 3Â°C difference, improve airflow. Also, keep the evaporator coils clean. Dust and ice block airflow. Defrost regularly. A well-designed airflow system saves energy and keeps products fresh. Remember, cold air must go everywhereâif it can't, your cold room isn't working.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cold Storage Design and Layout for African Agribusiness

Cold storage is one of the highest-leverage investments a horticultural, dairy, meat, or floriculture business can make in Africa. A well-designed room protects 20â40% of post-harvest value that is otherwise lost to heat, ethylene, moisture, and rough handling. But a poorly designed room â wrong orientation, thin insulation, leaky doors, blocked airflow â burns electricity, fails to hold temperature, and destroys the very produce it was built to protect.

This practical reference condenses the six core lessons of this module into decision-ready guidance: site selection and orientation, insulation, vapor barriers and air tightness, flooring and drainage, racking configurations, and airflow design. Treat it as your on-site checklist and design brief. It is written for the realities of African operations â unreliable grid power, hot ambient conditions, high humidity in coastal and tropical zones, dusty environments, and cost-sensitive capital budgets.

1. Site Selection and Orientation

Site selection is a business decision before it is an engineering one. Your cold room must sit close to production, close to a reliable power source, and on ground that will not flood. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, ambient temperatures routinely exceed 35Â°C and solar radiation is intense; every design choice must reduce heat load, not add to it.

Key site criteria:

  • Proximity to harvest point: Shorten the time between harvest and cooling. Every hour at ambient temperature reduces shelf life. Aim for less than 2 hours from field to pre-cooling where possible.
  • Power reliability: Site near a stable grid connection or plan for solar hybrid and generator backup. Cold rooms are power-critical infrastructure.
  • Elevation and drainage: Avoid flood-prone lowlands. The floor must be above the surrounding water table and graded to shed surface water.
  • Access for vehicles: Loading bays must accommodate the largest truck that will serve the facility, with turning space and a level apron.
  • Orientation: In the northern hemisphere tropics, orient the building so the longest wall faces away from the afternoon sun (west). In the southern hemisphere, avoid direct west and north exposure. Minimize glazing on sun-facing walls. Where possible, use the building's own mass and adjacent structures as shade.
  • Future expansion: Leave land for additional rooms, a pre-cooling bay, and a staging area.

In coastal West Africa and East African port cities, humidity and salt-laden air demand corrosion-resistant materials and robust vapor control. In the Sahel and semi-arid zones, dust infiltration and extreme diurnal temperature swings are the dominant threats.

2. Insulation Materials and Thickness

Insulation is the single biggest determinant of energy consumption in a cold room. In African conditions, under-insulation is the most common and most expensive mistake. The goal is to keep heat out â not just to keep cold in.

Common insulation materials:

  • Polyurethane (PU) panels: The industry standard for cold rooms. High R-value per inch, good structural rigidity, available as pre-fabricated panels with cam-locks. Typical density 40 kg/mÂ³.
  • Polyisocyanurate (PIR): Slightly better fire performance than PU, similar thermal performance.
  • Expanded polystyrene (EPS): Cheaper but lower R-value and moisture-sensitive. Acceptable for chill rooms in dry climates, not recommended for freezer rooms or humid zones.
  • Mineral wool / rock wool: Fire-resistant but heavier and requires separate vapor barrier. Used in some industrial builds.

Thickness guidance (typical, for 30â35Â°C ambient):

Table 1: Indicative insulation thickness by room type and ambient temperature
Room Type Set Point Walls (PU/PIR) Ceiling (PU/PIR) Floor (where insulated)
Chill room (fruit & veg) 0 to +8Â°C 75â100 mm 100â125 mm 75â100 mm
Banana ripening room +14 to +18Â°C 75 mm 75â100 mm 50â75 mm
Meat / dairy chill 0 to +4Â°C 100 mm 100â125 mm 100 mm
Freezer / frozen storage -18 to -25Â°C 150â200 mm 150â200 mm 150â200 mm

Source: Adapted from ASHRAE Handbook â Refrigeration (2022) and FAO post-harvest cold chain guidance.

Rule of thumb: if you are unsure, go thicker. The incremental cost of 25 mm of PU is small compared to years of excess electricity bills. In hot African climates, undersized insulation can increase compressor runtime by 30â50%.

3. Vapor Barriers and Air Tightness

Moisture is the silent killer of cold rooms. Warm, humid air migrating into the insulation condenses, degrades thermal performance, causes corrosion, and can freeze into ice that damages panels. Air leakage does the same â every gap, every poorly sealed penetration, every worn door gasket is a pathway for heat and moisture.

Design principles:

  • Vapor barrier on the warm side: The barrier must be on the exterior (warm) side of the insulation in hot climates, preventing moisture from entering the insulation from outside. In PU/PIR panels, the foam itself is a vapor retarder; joints must be sealed.
  • Continuous sealed envelope: All panel joints, penetrations (pipes, cables, drains), and door frames must be sealed with appropriate mastic, foam, or gaskets.
  • Air-tight doors: Use high-quality door gaskets, door closers, and where traffic is heavy, air curtains or strip curtains. In African facilities, strip curtains are cost-effective and greatly reduce infiltration.
  • Pressure relief: Freezer rooms need pressure relief valves to prevent panel damage during defrost and temperature swings.
  • Regular inspection: Gaskets and seals deteriorate in heat and dust. Inspect monthly.

4. Flooring and Drainage Systems

The floor must carry forklift and pallet loads, resist moisture, and drain wash-down water and condensate. In Africa, floors are often the weakest point â cracked, uneven, or poorly drained, leading to ice buildup, slips, and sanitation failures.

Floor design requirements:

  • Load-bearing: Reinforced concrete slab designed for the racking and forklift loads. Typically 150â200 mm thick with mesh or rebar.
  • Insulation (freezer rooms): Insulated floor with a vapor barrier beneath and a heated or ventilated sub-floor to prevent frost heave.
  • Slope and drainage: Floor should slope 1:100 to 1:150 toward drainage points. Use trapped floor drains with removable strainers, and ensure drains do not allow warm air or pests to enter.
  • Sanitation: Smooth, non-porous, easily cleaned surface. Epoxy or hardened concrete with a sealed finish.
  • Condensate management: Evaporator drain lines must be trapped, insulated, and sloped to a discharge point. Blocked drains are a leading cause of ice and water damage.

5. Racking and Storage Configurations

Racking is not just storage â it is airflow infrastructure. The way you stack pallets determines whether cold air reaches every product or whether you create hot spots that shorten shelf life.

Configuration options:

  • Selective racking: Single-deep pallet positions, 100% accessibility. Best for high-turnover, mixed-SKU operations. Requires more aisle space.
  • Drive-in / drive-through: High-density storage for homogeneous, low-turnover products. Poor airflow if over-filled.
  • Push-back / pallet flow: Medium-density, good for FIFO. Higher capital cost.
  • Block stacking: Cheapest but worst for airflow and traceability. Only for short-term, robust products.

Airflow-critical rules:

  • Maintain at least 100â150 mm clearance between pallets and walls.
  • Maintain 300â450 mm clearance between the top of the stack and the ceiling or evaporator discharge.
  • Align racking so aisles run parallel to the evaporator airflow direction.
  • Never block evaporator intake or discharge with pallets or boxes.
  • Use pallets with adequate openings (not solid sheets) to allow vertical airflow where required.
Table 2: Recommended clearances for cold room airflow and access
Location Minimum Clearance Notes
Wall to pallet 100â150 mm Prevents condensation and allows air movement
Ceiling to top of stack 300â450 mm Critical for evaporator throw and return
Evaporator to nearest pallet â¥ 1,000 mm Prevents short-cycling and uneven cooling
Floor to bottom of pallet 100 mm Allows cleaning and air circulation
Aisle width (forklift) 2,500â3,500 mm Depends on forklift type and racking

Source: Adapted from IIR (International Institute of Refrigeration) cold store design guidance and FAO cold chain manuals.

6. Designing for Efficient Airflow

Airflow is how a cold room actually cools product. The refrigeration system cools air; the air must then reach every product. Poor airflow creates warm pockets, condensation, and uneven quality. Good airflow design is about throw, return, and obstruction management.

Design rules for airflow:

  • Position evaporators to throw air along the ceiling and return along the floor, creating a circular pattern.
  • Do not place racking directly in front of the evaporator discharge â allow at least 1 m.
  • Keep aisles clear and aligned with airflow.
  • Use forced-air units with adequate throw for the room length; for long rooms, use multiple units or ducted distribution.
  • Ensure product is not stacked above the evaporator return path.
  • Monitor temperature at multiple points â top, bottom, corners â not just at the thermostat.
â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Refrigerant and Confined Space Hazards

Cold rooms are confined spaces. Refrigerants used in cold storage â including ammonia (R717), R404A, R134a, and R290 (propane) â can cause asphyxiation, frostbite, or fire. Never enter a cold room alone. Ensure ventilation, refrigerant leak detection, and emergency exits are in place. Ammonia systems require specific PPE and training. All electrical work must comply with local codes and be done by qualified personnel. In African contexts where maintenance skills may be scarce, invest in training and clear emergency procedures before commissioning.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Site: High ground, flood-safe, close to harvest and power, with room to expand.
  2. Orientation: Minimize west and sun-facing wall exposure; use shade and building mass.
  3. Insulation: PU/PIR panels, 100 mm minimum for chill, 150â200 mm for freezer, thicker in hot climates.
  4. Vapor and air sealing: Continuous warm-side barrier, sealed joints, quality gaskets, strip curtains on busy doors.
  5. Floor: Reinforced, sloped 1:100â1:150, drained, insulated in freezer rooms, easy to clean.
  6. Racking: 100â150 mm wall clearance, 300â450 mm ceiling clearance, aisles aligned with airflow.
  7. Airflow: Evaporator throw along ceiling, return along floor, no obstructions, multi-point temperature monitoring.
  8. Safety and maintenance: Refrigerant detection, confined-space procedures, monthly gasket and drain checks, trained staff.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Design and Operation of Cold Stores (free full text)
  • FAO â Small-Scale Cold Storage for Horticultural Produce
  • ASHRAE Handbook â Refrigeration (see library or institutional access)
  • IIR â International Institute of Refrigeration (FRIDOC database, free abstracts)
  • U.S. DOE â Refrigeration Systems and Cold Storage Efficiency Resources

Business takeaway: In African agribusiness, cold storage design is not a technical afterthought â it is a profit center. Every millimeter of insulation, every sealed joint, every centimeter of clearance, and every degree of airflow directly affects shelf life, energy cost, and customer trust. Design it right once, and the room pays for itself many times over.

quiz.q: Why is it important to avoid low-lying areas when selecting a site for a cold room?
options: A) They are more expensive to buy
B) They flood during rains, causing rust and insulation damage
D) They are harder to secure
quiz.explanation: Flooding around the foundation leads to rust and insulation damage.

quiz.q: In Africa, which orientation of the longest walls helps reduce direct sun exposure?
options: D) Any orientation, it doesn't matter
quiz.explanation: North and south walls receive less direct sun in most African locations.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of placing the cold room door in the shade?
options: B) It stays cooler and opens less often
quiz.explanation: A shaded door stays cooler, reducing heat gain and opening frequency.

quiz.q: What should you check with local authorities before building a cold room?
options: A) The color of the building
C) The height of the fence
quiz.explanation: Permits are often required for commercial refrigeration to avoid fines.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good reason to visit a potential site at different times of day?
options: A) To see sun and water patterns
C) To check the soil type
quiz.explanation: Visiting at different times helps assess sun exposure and water drainage.

quiz.q: What is the most common insulation material for cold rooms in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Polyurethane foam is widely used due to its high R-value and availability.

quiz.q: For a freezer (-18Â°C to -25Â°C), what thickness of polyurethane insulation is recommended?
quiz.explanation: Freezers require thicker insulation (100â150 mm) to handle the larger temperature difference.

quiz.q: What is the R-value of polyurethane foam per inch?
quiz.explanation: Polyurethane has an R-value of about 6 per inch, making it a good insulator.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid compressing insulation during installation?
quiz.explanation: Compressing insulation reduces its thickness and thus its R-value.

quiz.q: What is a sign that insulation may be of poor quality?
options: A) It is white in color
B) It warps or smells when left in the sun
quiz.explanation: Warping or smelling indicates poor quality and potential failure.

quiz.q: Where should a vapor barrier be installed?
options: A) On the cold side of the insulation
B) On the warm side of the insulation
C) In the middle of the insulation
quiz.explanation: The vapor barrier goes on the warm side to stop moisture from entering the insulation.

quiz.q: What is a common material for a vapor barrier?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum foil or polyethylene plastic sheets are common vapor barriers.

quiz.q: How much should you overlap vapor barrier sheets?
quiz.explanation: Overlap at least 150 mm to ensure a continuous barrier.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for air leaks in a cold room?
quiz.explanation: A smoke test (e.g., with incense) reveals air leaks by movement of smoke.

quiz.q: What can a 1 mm gap around a door do to your energy bill?
quiz.explanation: Even a small gap can add about 10% to energy costs due to air infiltration.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for a cold room floor toward a drain?
quiz.explanation: A 1% slope (1 cm per meter) allows proper drainage without being too steep.

quiz.q: Why is under-floor insulation important for a freezer?
options: A) To prevent frost heave and heat gain
B) To make the floor softer
quiz.explanation: Under-floor insulation prevents frost heave and reduces heat gain from the ground.

quiz.q: What type of floor finish is recommended for a cold room?
quiz.explanation: Sealed concrete or epoxy is durable, easy to clean, and resists moisture.

quiz.q: What is a key feature of a floor drain in a cold room?
options: A) It should be at the highest point
B) It should have a trap to prevent sewer gases
C) It should be 25 mm diameter
D) It should be made of plastic
quiz.explanation: A trap prevents sewer gases from entering the cold room.

quiz.q: Why should you keep the floor dry near doors?
quiz.explanation: Dry floors prevent ice, slips, and excess humidity.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended clearance between stored products and the floor?
quiz.explanation: At least 100 mm off the floor allows air circulation and cleaning.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid wooden racks in a cold room?
options: C) They are not strong enough
D) They are hard to clean
quiz.explanation: Wood can absorb moisture and grow mold in humid cold rooms.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for heavy items in a cold room?
options: A) Store them on top shelves
B) Store them on lower shelves
C) Store them near the door
D) Store them in the center
quiz.explanation: Heavy items should be stored low for safety and ease of handling.

quiz.q: What percentage of the cold room volume should be left empty for air circulation?
quiz.explanation: Leaving at least 30% empty ensures proper air movement and prevents warm spots.

quiz.q: What is the recommended aisle width for trolleys in a cold room?
quiz.explanation: At least 1 meter allows safe and efficient movement of trolleys.

quiz.q: Where should the evaporator unit be positioned for efficient airflow?
options: B) At one end, blowing along the ceiling or aisle
C) In the center of the room
quiz.explanation: Positioning at one end allows air to circulate throughout the room.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap between the top of racks and the ceiling?
quiz.explanation: At least 300 mm allows air to flow over the racks.

quiz.q: How many air changes per hour are recommended for a chiller?
quiz.explanation: Chillers typically need 10â20 air changes per hour for even cooling.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a strip curtain on a cold room door?
options: B) To reduce warm air infiltration
D) To save on door costs
quiz.explanation: Strip curtains reduce warm air entering when the door is open.

quiz.q: What should you do if you notice a 3Â°C temperature difference in different parts of your cold room?
quiz.explanation: A 3Â°C difference indicates poor airflow, so you should improve circulation.
